title: working 2
content:
Your apps found the gaps because they use features the way real apps do. Nearly every recent bug sits on an
  item the scorecard counted as covered:                              
  - CollectionView was "covered" while three things were broken: template selectors, view-based empty views,
    and controls inside rows.
  - ScrollView was "covered" while it took the full height instead of its content's.
  - Toast and Snackbar "complete their API contract": the test only checks that the call finishes. Nothing in
    it checks that anything appears on screen.

  What I measured just now:
  - Property mappings: for each of the 58 controls we map, I compared MAUI's own handler mappings with ours.
    MAUI defines 2,135 and 107 have no Linux equivalent. A mapped property can still behave wrongly (the
    template-selector bug was on a mapped one), so this is a floor, not a guarantee. The biggest gaps:
    - CollectionView: IsGrouped, HeaderTemplate, FooterTemplate, ItemSizingStrategy, CanReorderItems
    - SearchBar: 11 entry properties (Keyboard, MaxLength, IsReadOnly, ...)
    - BoxView and all shapes: stroke dash, line cap and join
    - Label, Entry, Editor and Button: TextTransform
    - Pickers: IsOpen
    - Slider: ThumbImageSource
    - RefreshView: IsRefreshEnabled
  - Third-party stubs: I compared each library's platform-neutral build (what Linux gets) with its Windows
    build. Many of the methods it found are native plumbing the Syncfusion bridge already replaces, so the
    list is for triage, not a bug count.
    - It flags the exact bugs we found by hand: IconTintColorBehavior, SfListView's layout call, and
      PdfToImageConverter.
    - It also flags things nobody has looked at yet:
      - CommunityToolkit's TouchBehavior, which has no Linux implementation at all;
      - SfPopup's screen-size methods, which return 0; 
      - SfListView's keyboard listener;
      - SfPdfViewer's pan/zoom and desktop layout;
      - MAUI's ViewHandler.SetupContainer, which is how clipping and shadow wrappers get attached on Windows.
      
  What better coverage needs, by value for effort:
  1. Gate on MAUI's own mappings. Turn the mapper comparison into a test that fails when MAUI adds a property
     we don't handle, with a reviewed list of deliberate exceptions. It's cheap, and it would have caught
     ShouldLoopPlayback, EmptyViewTemplate and the Shell toolbar items.
  2. Run MAUI's own handler tests. dotnet/maui's device tests check every handler property against the native
     view, through a small helper per platform that reads values back. Writing the Linux helpers lets MAUI's
     assertions become our specification, instead of tests we write from our own reading. This is the biggest
     step towards real parity, at medium-to-high effort.
  3. Compare layouts against Windows. Run one gallery app on your Windows runner and on Linux at the same
     window size, dump every element's frame through the inspector, and diff them. This catches layout bugs
     our own tests can't, because the expected values come from Windows rather than from us: ScrollView
     height, Grid star rows, stack orientation, the Shell title.
  4. Check invariants on every page of the samples and your apps, walked through the inspector. It's cheap to
     add and generic. It would have caught several recent bugs:
     - nothing draws outside its bounds unless the control allows it (would have caught both AspectFill bugs);
     - every visible, enabled interactive element can be hit at its centre (the CollectionView row and
       empty-view buttons);
     - no binding failures (the BindingContext overwrite);
     - no first-chance exceptions while pages load (the early Loaded).
  5. Scan libraries for stubs in CI, at the versions apps actually use. The compat suite pins Syncfusion
     34.2.9 while CiteLynq runs 35.1.37. Each finding would be marked "covered by the bridge" or "open", so a
     new library version shows up as a diff to review.
  6. Make the scorecard finer-grained. Split items per feature as MAUI's docs list them. For CollectionView
     that means separate items for template selectors, grouping, header and footer, empty view, selection
     modes, grid layout, scroll-to and remaining-items. 125/125 then becomes a number that has to be earned.

  I'd start with 1, 4 and 5. They're mostly automation and would have caught most of what your apps found.
  Then fix the CollectionView grouping, header and footer gaps and TouchBehavior, since real apps hit those
  first. Number 2 is the long-term answer for "parity with .NET MAUI".

  The scanner I built for this is in the scratchpad. I removed the one-off mapping comparison from the tests,
  so nothing in the repo changed. I can write this up as a page if you want to share it.
